title: UNIT 6: POPULATION & NATURAL RESOURCES
notes:
✓ Population ecology studies how populations change, grow, interact and respond to their environment.

→ Natural resources are materials supplied by nature that support life and human activities.

title: 6.1 POPULATION ECOLOGY
notes:
✓ Population ecology = study of the distribution, abundance, interactions and changes of populations in their environment.

→ Population → group of individuals of the same species living and interbreeding in a given area.

◆ Population size (N) → total number of individuals.

◆ Population density → number of individuals per unit area/volume.

◆ Dispersal → pattern of spacing of individuals within a population.

title: 6.1.1 POPULATION SIZE, DENSITY & DISPERSAL
notes:
✓ Population size = total individuals (N).

→ Population density = individuals ÷ area/volume.

✓ Dispersion patterns:

◆ Clumped → individuals occur in groups.
◆ Uniform → individuals are evenly spaced.
◆ Random → no predictable spacing.

→ Population size can be estimated using sampling methods.

title: POPULATION STUDY: QUADRAT METHOD
notes:
✓ Used mainly for plants and other immobile/slow-moving organisms.

1 Place quadrats randomly in the habitat.
2 Count individuals inside each quadrat.
3 Use the sample to estimate population size and density.

◆ Quadrat = square sampling area made from sticks, string, wood, plastic or metal.

title: MARK–RECAPTURE METHOD
notes:
✓ Used mainly for mobile animals.

1 Capture and mark a sample → release.
2 Later capture another sample.
3 Count marked individuals in the second sample.
4 Estimate total population.

→ Common formula: N ≈ (M × n) ÷ X

◆ M = initially marked; n = second sample; X = marked individuals recaptured.

title: 6.1.2 EXPONENTIAL & LOGISTIC GROWTH
notes:
✓ Population growth depends on births, deaths, immigration and emigration.

→ Exponential growth → resources assumed unlimited; J-shaped curve.
→ Logistic growth → resources limited; S-shaped curve.
→ Carrying capacity (K) → maximum population an environment can sustainably support.

◆ Exponential: rapid continuous increase.
◆ Logistic: growth slows as population approaches K.

title: POPULATION GROWTH RATE
notes:
✓ Intrinsic rate of natural increase = r.

→ r > 0 → population increases
→ r = 0 → zero population growth
→ r < 0 → population decreases

✓ Exponential model:
dN/dt = rN

✓ Logistic model:
dN/dt = rN(K−N)/K

◆ N = population size; r = intrinsic growth rate; K = carrying capacity.

title: 6.1.3 DEMOGRAPHIC STRUCTURE
notes:
✓ Demography = study of population characteristics and changes.

✓ Important demographic parameters:
◆ Birth rate → live births per 1,000 people/year.
◆ Death rate → deaths per 1,000 people/year.
◆ Infant mortality → deaths of infants under 1 year per 1,000 live births.
◆ Fertility rate → number of children born.
◆ Mortality rate → rate of death.
◆ Life expectancy → expected years of life.
◆ Migration → movement of people.
◆ Immigration → movement into an area.
◆ Emigration → movement out of an area.

title: POPULATION PYRAMIDS
notes:
✓ Population pyramid = graph showing age-sex composition.

◆ Expansive → broad base; many young people; high growth potential.

◆ Stationary → similar proportions across age groups; little/no growth.

◆ Constrictive → smaller young population; slow or negative growth.

→ Used to predict population growth and future needs such as schools, hospitals and housing.

title: SURVIVORSHIP CURVES
notes:
✓ Survivorship curve = graph showing survival of individuals at different ages.

◆ Type I → few offspring + high parental care; low early mortality; humans and most mammals.

◆ Type II → fairly constant mortality at all ages; some birds.

◆ Type III → many offspring + little care; high early mortality; many plants, fish and invertebrates.

title: 6.1.4 POPULATION REGULATION
notes:
✓ Population regulation = factors that limit population growth and keep populations near carrying capacity.

→ Density-dependent factors → effects increase as population density increases.
◆ Examples: competition, predation, disease, waste accumulation.

→ Density-independent factors → affect populations regardless of density.
◆ Examples: weather, drought, floods, earthquakes, natural disasters and pollution.

title: 6.2 NATURAL RESOURCES
notes:
✓ Natural resources = naturally occurring materials used by organisms and humans.

◆ Examples: water, sunlight, plants, animals, soil, minerals, oil, coal and natural gas.

✓ Main classifications:
◆ Renewable
◆ Non-renewable
◆ Exhaustible
◆ Inexhaustible

title: 6.2.1 RENEWABLE RESOURCES
notes:
✓ Renewable resources can naturally be replaced or replenished after use.

◆ Examples: sunlight, wind, water, trees, tidal energy, biomass and hydropower.

→ Renewable does not mean unlimited: overuse and poor management can cause depletion.

title: 6.2.2 NON-RENEWABLE RESOURCES
notes:
✓ Non-renewable resources replenish extremely slowly and may take millions of years to form.

◆ Examples: fossil fuels, coal, natural gas and minerals.

→ If consumption is faster than natural recovery, the resource becomes depleted.

title: 6.3 CONSERVATION OF NATURAL RESOURCES IN ETHIOPIA
notes:
✓ Conservation = protection and wise management of natural resources so they remain available for present and future generations.

✓ Important conservation areas include:
◆ Soil
◆ Water
◆ Forests
◆ Wildlife
◆ Crop genetic resources

→ Ethiopia uses protected areas such as national parks, wildlife sanctuaries, wildlife reserves and community conservation areas.

title: SOIL & WATER CONSERVATION
notes:
✓ Major problems: soil erosion, declining water quantity and declining water quality.

→ Causes → deforestation, poor land management, household waste and industrial waste.

✓ Mechanical measures:
◆ Bunds
◆ Terraces
◆ Diversion ditches
◆ Check dams
◆ Micro-basins
◆ Hillside terraces

✓ Biological measures:
◆ Agroforestry
◆ Afforestation
◆ Tree planting
◆ Protecting degraded land

→ Green Legacy is an Ethiopian example of environmental restoration.

title: WILDLIFE CONSERVATION
notes:
✓ Protected areas conserve biodiversity and wildlife.

◆ National park → protects natural ecosystems and wildlife.
◆ Wildlife sanctuary → protects particular wildlife/species and habitat.
◆ Wildlife reserve → protects wildlife and habitat under controlled management.
◆ Community conservation area → conservation involving local communities.

→ Ethiopia has diverse endemic plants and is an important centre of crop genetic diversity.

title: 6.5.1 ENVIRONMENTAL POLLUTION
notes:
✓ Pollution = contamination of the environment that disrupts normal environmental processes.

✓ Types:
◆ Air pollution
◆ Water pollution
◆ Land pollution
◆ Noise pollution
◆ Light pollution

→ Pollution occurs when harmful substances/energy enter the environment faster than natural processes can disperse, decompose or recycle them.

title: AIR POLLUTION
notes:
✓ Air pollution = harmful gases, particles, dust and smoke contaminating the atmosphere.

✓ Major pollutants:
◆ CO → carbon monoxide
◆ NO₂ → nitrogen dioxide
◆ O₃ → ozone
◆ SO₂ → sulfur dioxide
◆ Lead
◆ Smog
◆ Particulate matter

→ Sources → vehicles, industries, burning coal/natural gas, refrigerants and volatile chemicals.

title: WATER POLLUTION
notes:
✓ Water pollution = contamination of water bodies by harmful substances.

→ Causes → industrial/agricultural waste, sewage, oil, fertilizers, insecticides, herbicides, pathogens and invasive water plants such as water hyacinth (Emboch).

→ Effects → fish decline, biodiversity loss and waterborne diseases.

◆ Eutrophication → excessive nutrient enrichment causing rapid algal/plant growth and reduced water quality.

title: 6.5.2 CLIMATE CHANGE
notes:
✓ Climate = usual weather pattern of a place.
✓ Climate change = long-term change in normal weather patterns such as temperature and rainfall.

✓ Causes:
◆ Natural → volcanic activity, solar variation, energy/water/carbon changes.
◆ Human → fossil-fuel combustion and increased greenhouse gases.

→ Important greenhouse gases → CO₂, methane (CH₄), nitrous oxide (N₂O) and fluorinated gases.

title: 6.5.3 GLOBAL WARMING
notes:
✓ Global warming = increase in Earth's average temperature, mainly driven by increased greenhouse gases from human activities.

→ Greenhouse effect → greenhouse gases absorb/trap outgoing heat.

✓ Effects:
◆ Melting ice
◆ Rising sea levels
◆ Drought
◆ Flooding
◆ Species extinction
◆ Heat stress
◆ Health problems
◆ Poverty and displacement

title: 6.5.4 OZONE LAYER DEPLETION
notes:
✓ Ozone layer = O₃-rich region mainly in the stratosphere that absorbs harmful UV radiation.

→ Major causes → CFCs, HCFCs and halons.

→ Chlorine released from CFCs participates in catalytic reactions that destroy ozone.

✓ Effects:
◆ Skin cancer
◆ Cataracts
◆ Weakened immunity
◆ Damage to plants and animals
◆ Increased ground-level ozone/smog

→ Atmospheric layers: Troposphere → Stratosphere → Mesosphere → Thermosphere.

title: 6.5.5 ACID RAIN
notes:
✓ Acid rain = precipitation with a lower pH than normal rain.

✓ Main pollutants:
◆ SO₂ → sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄)
◆ NO₂/NOₓ → nitric acid (HNO₃)
◆ CO₂ → carbonic acid (H₂CO₃)

→ Sources → fossil-fuel combustion, industries, power plants and vehicle engines.

✓ Effects → damages plants, acidifies soil/water, harms aquatic organisms, corrodes buildings and can affect human health.

title: 6.5.6 LOSS OF BIODIVERSITY
notes:
✓ Biodiversity = variety of life at genetic, species and ecosystem/community levels.

✓ Major causes:
◆ Habitat loss/degradation
◆ Habitat fragmentation
◆ Overexploitation
◆ Pollution
◆ Climate change
◆ Invasive species

→ Effects → species extinction, ecosystem instability and reduced food, water, fertile soil and ecosystem services.

title: 6.5.7 TOXIC BIOACCUMULATION
notes:
✓ Bioaccumulation = gradual buildup of a toxic substance inside an organism.

→ Biomagnification = increasing concentration of a persistent toxic substance at higher trophic levels.

◆ Example: DDT can accumulate through food chains and affect birds of prey by weakening eggshells.

→ Higher trophic levels generally receive greater concentrations of persistent toxins.

title: 6.5.8 RESOURCE DEPLETION
notes:
✓ Resource depletion = resources are consumed faster than they can recover, causing scarcity.

✓ Major causes:
◆ Overpopulation
◆ Poor farming practices
◆ Overconsumption
◆ Excessive mineral/oil extraction
◆ Industrial and technological development
◆ Overuse of pesticides and chemicals

→ Effects → scarcity, soil degradation, reduced productivity and loss of natural resources.

title: 6.6 INDIGENOUS CONSERVATION PRACTICES IN ETHIOPIA
notes:
✓ Indigenous knowledge = locally developed knowledge, skills and practices used to manage natural resources and the environment.

✓ Ethiopian conservation practices include:
◆ Soil conservation
◆ Water conservation
◆ Forest conservation
◆ Crop-seed selection and preservation
◆ Medicinal-plant conservation
◆ Animal/wildlife conservation

→ The Konso people are highlighted as an important example of indigenous conservation knowledge.

title: KONSО & INDIGENOUS CONSERVATION
notes:
✓ Important approaches include protecting degraded land, tree planting, agroforestry, afforestation and traditional soil/water-management practices.

◆ Agroforestry → integrating trees with crops/livestock.
◆ Afforestation → establishing trees/forest where there was little or no forest.
◆ Conservation → sustainable protection and use of resources.

→ Indigenous knowledge combines environmental practices with community rules, social values and local experience.

title: KEY TERMS TO REMEMBER
notes:
◆ Population → same-species individuals in an area.
◆ Population ecology → study of population changes and interactions.
◆ Population size (N) → total individuals.
◆ Population density → individuals per unit area/volume.
◆ Dispersal → spacing pattern of individuals.
◆ Quadrat → square sampling area.
◆ Mark-recapture → estimating mobile-animal populations.
◆ Demography → study of population characteristics/dynamics.
◆ Carrying capacity (K) → maximum sustainable population size.
◆ Intrinsic growth rate (r) → per-capita natural population growth rate.
◆ Zero population growth → r = 0.
◆ Immigration → movement into an area.
◆ Emigration → movement out.
◆ Population pyramid → age-sex population graph.
◆ Survivorship curve → survival pattern across age.
◆ Density-dependent → regulation affected by population density.
◆ Density-independent → regulation independent of density.
◆ Natural resource → useful naturally occurring material.
◆ Renewable → naturally replenishable resource.
◆ Non-renewable → slowly replenished resource.
◆ Conservation → protection and wise management of resources.
◆ Pollution → harmful environmental contamination.
◆ Climate change → change in usual climate patterns.
◆ Global warming → rise in Earth's average temperature.
◆ Greenhouse effect → trapping of heat by greenhouse gases.
◆ Ozone depletion → reduction of stratospheric ozone.
◆ Acid rain → unusually acidic precipitation.
◆ Biodiversity → variety of genes, species and ecosystems.
◆ Bioaccumulation → toxin buildup within an organism.
◆ Biomagnification → toxin concentration increases up food chains.
◆ Resource depletion → resource use exceeds recovery.
◆ Indigenous knowledge → locally developed environmental knowledge and practices.
